title: Citizenship
hookLine: pray for those in authority (1 Timothy 2:1–2), and seek the common good
tomorrow: is justice helping one person, or fixing the whole road?

cards: Any town's group chat about the next council meeting has more opinions than members. Here's an older, stranger letter about a city.
The prophet Jeremiah writes to his people, carried off as captives to Babylon, the empire that burned Jerusalem's temple. Other prophets are telling them: hold on, you'll be home soon.
Jeremiah writes instead: “seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it.” Pray for Babylon? Why would captives do that?

teach.b: The answer is the end of the same verse: “for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.” Their good is tied up with their neighbors' good.
So Jeremiah tells them to build houses, plant gardens, eat what grows, raise families. Live there for real, not with one foot out the door.
The peace he means is shalom: not just quiet, but a city made whole.

teach.h: PRAYERS FOR ALL, AND FOR RULERS.
teach.b: The First Letter to Timothy says something close, to Christians living under emperors: “supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men; For kings, and for all that are in authority.”
Notice the order. For all people first; then for those in charge. Notice, too, what this isn't.
It isn't approval of every ruler, and it isn't a party platform; Christians disagree about policies, and the prayer comes before any of that.

It's simpler and harder: wanting good for the place you live and the people who run it, including the ones you didn't choose. Captives planting gardens in the city that took them. That's the puzzle solved.

how: The Book of Common Prayer includes prayers for rulers and all in authority, and other churches pray for leaders in their own ways; Christians also serve their towns as voters, volunteers and officials.

o: belonging to a place and wanting its good
keeping faith out of public life entirely
agreeing with every leader the city picks

games.q: a letter to the city — tap the pairs.
p: prayers for all, and for kings

s: Jeremiah told the captives to keep apart from Babylon and wait
he told them to build, plant, and seek the city's peace.
praying for leaders means approving of everything they do
the letter asks prayers for all in authority; it isn't a verdict on them.
Jeremiah ties the captives' peace to the city's peace
for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.

games.q: the student body president you campaigned against wins, and she's planning the senior trip. what fits Jeremiah's letter?
o: want the trip to go well, and help where you can.
pray for her quietly, but don't lift a finger to help.
sit this one out until the next election comes around.
games.why: seek the peace of the city, Jeremiah wrote to captives in Babylon: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace. prayer and help go together.

practice: Write the name of your town or city on a scrap of paper, and under it the name of one person who leads it: a mayor, a principal, a council member. Add one good thing you want for them both.
If you pray, pray for them by name; if not, hold that good in mind for the sit.

wordCard.voice: Citizenship. Belonging to a place and wanting its good, because your peace is tied to its peace.

orig.note: Hebrew: peace, wholeness, well-being. 'the peace of the city' in Jeremiah 29:7.

carryVoice: Carry this: seek the city's peace, even in a city you never chose. Until tomorrow.
